slides.0.title: Level 1 final assessment
slides.0.subtitle: The language of service: confirm, temperature, timing, reasons
slides.1.title: Level 1 key points
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Service sequence
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Present and confirm the label → cut the foil, open quietly → host tastes → serve in order, host last; for sparkling turn the bottle, 45 degrees, thumb on cork; replace faulty bottles politely
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Temperature and decanting
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Sparkling and sweet about 6–10°C, whites about 7–13°C, reds about 13–18°C; decant to remove sediment or to aerate; cellar a steady 12–14°C
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Lists and pairing
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Lists match the menu and stay current; lower multiples on expensive wines; watch oxidation by the glass; sweetness, umami, heat and bitterness harden wine, salt and acid soften it; acid cuts fat, tannin suits protein
slides.1.content: The key to service exams: every action has a reason and every recommendation a principle.
slides.2.componentProps.slide.title: 📋 Level 1 final assessment
What is the main purpose of the host tasting?
B. To decide whether to pay
Roughly how cold should sparkling wine be served?
Low temperature keeps the mousse fine.
How should Vintage Port be handled before opening?
C. Stand it upright, then decant off the sediment
Vintage Port ages in bottle and often has sediment.
What does an umami-rich dish do to wine?
A. Makes it seem more bitter, astringent and acidic
A little salt or acid helps.
What is a common rule of thumb for pricing by the glass?
A. Same price as the bottle
B. One glass roughly covers the bottle’s cost
C. Sell a glass at cost
D. The first glass is free
To offset the risk of oxidation after opening.
A. Barolo is low in alcohol
C. Tannin binds with protein and fat
Before recommending a wine, what should the sommelier find out first?
Then offer two or three options at different prices.
